thread.title_full: MSU Extension advises food businesses to conduct mock recalls for safety readiness

author: Great Lakes Wire
title: MSU Extension advises food businesses to conduct mock recalls for safety readiness
text:
Michigan State University Extension and the MSU Product Center advised on May 27 that packaged food and beverage businesses should prepare for potential product recalls by developing and testing recall plans through simulated exercises. The organizations say that conducting a mock recall can help protect businesses, customers, and brands by evaluating preparedness before an actual safety issue arises.
A mock recall is described as a simulated exercise designed to test a company’s ability to quickly identify, trace, and remove a product from the marketplace if needed. “Think of it as a fire drill for your food safety system. Instead of reacting during a real crisis, a mock recall allows you to evaluate your preparedness in a controlled environment before consumer safety and your reputation are at risk,” the guidance states.
The MSU Product Center said that regular practice with mock recalls helps test traceability systems, identify gaps in recordkeeping, strengthen response time, clarify team roles and communication procedures, and improve overall food safety readiness. A strong recall plan should include components such as designated teams, clear procedures for identifying problems and affected products, risk assessment protocols, communication plans for stakeholders including regulators and customers, methods for product recovery or control, robust recordkeeping systems tracking product movement both backward to suppliers and forward to customers or distributors, effectiveness checks during drills or real events, root cause investigation processes with corrective actions outlined clearly in documentation.
For high-risk foods—such as certain cheeses; shell eggs; nut butters; fresh herbs; leafy greens; fresh-cut fruits/vegetables; cucumbers; melons; peppers; tomatoes; sprouts; tropical fruits; finfish/shellfish; ready-to-eat deli salads—the U.S. Food & Drug Administration has established additional recordkeeping requirements under its Food Traceability Rule (21 CFR Part 1 Subpart S), finalized in November 2022. While the rule became effective January 2023, the FDA has proposed moving compliance deadlines to July 20, 2028. These rules aim at improving rapid traceback capabilities during outbreaks.
Common issues identified during implementation include reliance on generic plans not tailored to operations, incomplete accounting of materials (including packaging or locally sourced items), lack of comprehensive traceability testing in both directions, inability to reconcile finished products against raw materials used, and insufficient frequency or depth of mock recalls. Facilities are encouraged to run drills at least once per year—or more often if there are changes such as new products or suppliers—to ensure staff familiarity with all procedures involved.
The MSU Product Center offers guidance—including online courses—for Michigan entrepreneurs looking to strengthen their food safety programs. The center leverages Michigan State University’s expertise across agriculture, food, and natural resources sectors. According to the official website, the College of Agriculture and Natural Resources at Michigan State University addresses challenges in food health and environment through education, outreach, research centers, and extension services. It reported an enrollment of 3,735 students engaging over 340 scientists during fall 2021. The college collaborates through major research centers, focusing on sustainable practices while fostering student preparation.
